xref.title: Final Show (August 20, 2016)
xref.body: The band played their final show on August 20, 2016, in Kingston, their hometown. During this concert, Gord Downie notably called out the then-Prime Minister, who was present, to address the longstanding issues facing Canada's Indigenous people. "When the hit played their final show on August 20, 2016 in Kingston, Gord called out the Prime Minister by name who was there, suddenly demanding, okay, not so subtly, that he'd deal with these longstanding problems."

xref.title: Order of Canada for Indigenous Leadership (2017)
xref.body: In June 2017, Gord Downie was invested into the Order of Canada, not for his music (as The Hip already held that honor), but specifically for his leadership and advocacy on Indigenous issues. "In June 2017, Gord appeared in Ottawa for investment into the Order of Canada. Not for music, though, because the hip already had an order for that, but for his leadership with Indigenous issues."

xref.title: Activism Involvement
xref.body: The band became increasingly involved in activism as they grew. Their music blends traditional First Nations sounds with modern genres, often carrying messages relevant to Indigenous communities. "And the band grew from that and they became increasingly involved in activism."

xref.title: Adoption and Mi'kmaq Upbringing
xref.body: Although a member of the Piapot Plains Cree First Nation, Buffy was adopted and grew up in Massachusetts, with her adoptive parents being of Mi'kmaq descent, connecting her to multiple Indigenous traditions. "She is a member of the Piappot Plains Cree First Nation, but then she was adopted and grew up in Massachusetts, and those adopted parents were of Mick Mack to set."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Advocacy for Indigenous People
xref.body: Downie was a prominent supporter of Canada's Indigenous people, with his activism dating back to at least 2012 when the band participated in the Great Moon Gathering, an annual educational conference held by Indigenous communities along James Bay. He later helped publicize the horrors of the residential school program, particularly through the story of Chanie Wenjack. His work in this area, including the "Secret Path" project, became a major part of his legacy and quest for reconciliation. "Gord will also be remembered for his work and support of Canada's Indigenous people."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Birth and Early Activism
xref.body: Buffy Sainte-Marie was born in the Qu'Appelle Valley in Saskatchewan in 1941 and has been an activist for native causes for as long as she can remember, using her platform to advocate for Indigenous rights. "Buffy was born in the Capell Valley in Saskatchewan in 1941, and she's been an activist for native causes for as long as she can remember."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Brain Cancer Diagnosis and Death
xref.body: On May 24, 2016, it was announced that Gord Downie had been diagnosed with Gleoblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer. He passed away on the morning of October 17, 2017. Despite the short time remaining after his diagnosis, Downie dedicated his remaining months to tackling issues "so much bigger than him," particularly his advocacy for Indigenous people. "The news of Gord's death came out on the morning of October 17, 2017, because, as we all know, was Gleoblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Call to Action to the Prime Minister
xref.body: During The Tragically Hip's final show on August 20, 2016, in Kingston, Downie directly addressed the then-Prime Minister, who was in attendance, making an urgent demand for him to deal with longstanding problems faced by Indigenous people. "Gord called out the Prime Minister by name who was there, suddenly demanding, okay, not so subtly, that he'd deal with these longstanding problems."

xref.title: Collaboration with Buffy Sainte-Marie
xref.body: She provided vocals on the song "You Got to Run" from Buffy Sainte-Marie's 2017 album "Medicine Songs," bringing together two Polaris Prize-winning Indigenous Canadian artists. "This double shot is called You Got to Run. Two Indigenous Canadians, two Polaris Prize winners, Buffy St. Marie and Tanya Tagak, together on a 2017 song called You Got to Run."

xref.title: Enduring Legacy in Reconciliation
xref.body: Gord Downie's name is expected to be associated with reconciliation efforts for a significant period. His work to foster understanding between Indigenous peoples and other Canadians created a momentum that many hope will continue to grow. "Gord's name will be associated with reconciliation efforts for a long, long time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Environmental Activism
xref.body: The Tragically Hip were involved in various environmental programs and activities, including opposing the clear-cutting of old growth forests in British Columbia and advocating for clean water. Their activism led them to the Great Moon Gathering, an annual educational conference held by Indigenous communities along James Bay. In 2009, the band was part of the Swim Drink Fish Music Club, raising money to preserve clean rivers and lakes. "Gord and the hip were involved in many programs and activities, from opposing the clear-cutting of old growth forests and BC to making sure that we all have clean water."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Frontman's Nursing Career
xref.body: The band's sporadic activity led frontman Trevor Hurst to pursue a career in psychiatric nursing, working in an indigenous community and becoming an instructor. However, he had to quit nursing when the band seriously reactivated. "When a car line crush was seriously reactivated and started getting back to work, Trevor had to quit his nurse gig."

xref.title: Gord Downie's Post-Tour Work
xref.body: After the final tour, Gord Downie dedicated himself to new creative endeavors, writing and recording new music. He also committed significant effort to Canadian reconciliation initiatives with the country's Indigenous peoples. "After that gig, Gord plowed himself into work, writing and recording new music, and working hard on Canadian reconciliation efforts with its indigenous people."

xref.title: Historical Success for First Nations
xref.body: Radio play and record sales in their early career helped establish Kashtin as one of the most successful First Nations bands in Canadian history, paving the way for future Indigenous artists. xref.title: Indigenous Advocacy
xref.body: As he aged, Gord Downie deepened his involvement and concern for Canada's Indigenous people, which culminated in the establishment of the Chanie Wenjack Fund, dedicated to reconciliation between First Nations and other Canadians. "And the older he got, the deeper he got into the affairs and concerns of Canada's Indigenous people. This culminated with the establishment of the Cheney-Wenjack fun, a project dedicated to the supported reconciliation between the First Nations of Canada and the rest of us."

xref.title: Indigenous Recognition
xref.body: On December 6, 2016, Downie was awarded an Eagle Feather at the Assembly of First Nations and was given an honorary Aboriginal name, Wacapi Omane, which means "man who walked amongst the stars" in Lakota. He continued to speak out for Indigenous people, appearing in Ottawa on July 2, 2017. "On December 6, 2016, he was awarded an Eagle Feather at the Assembly of First Nations and given an honorary Aboriginal name, Wacapi Omane, which is Lakota for men who walked amongst the stars."

xref.title: Kayuga and Mohawk Heritage
xref.body: Robbie Robertson's mother was Kayuga and Mohawk, and she raised him on the Six Nations Reserve located west of Toronto. This strong connection to his Indigenous roots deeply influenced his later work. "His mom was a Kayuga and Mohawk raised on the Six Nations Reserve west of Toronto."

xref.body: Alien Weaponry is a Māori metal band originating from New Zealand. They are noted for being "really good," bringing Indigenous culture to the metal scene. "For example, there's a Mayori metal band from New Zealand called Alien Weaponry, who are really good."

xref.title: Pomo Heritage
xref.body: Chuck Billy, whose real name is Charles Billy, is the frontman of Testament. His father was Native American, specifically from the Pomo tribe, which is indigenous to Northern California. "Their frontman is a guy named Chuck Billy and that's his real name, Charles Billy. ... his father was Native American. He's of the Pomo, a tribe indigenous to Northern California."

xref.body: She was a regular on the children's television show *Sesame Street*, where she taught kids about native culture, bringing Indigenous traditions and perspectives to a young, mainstream audience. "She became a regular on Sesame Street, teaching kids about native culture."

xref.title: Social Activism
xref.body: The band was actively involved in various social causes, including environmental protection, social justice, equality, anti-racism, disaster relief for places like Haiti, feminist causes, decolonization, and issues concerning Canada's Indigenous people. "The hip was also involved in social activism tackling issues involving the environment, social justice, equality, racism, disaster relief for places like Haiti, feminist causes, decolonization, and issues involving Canada's indigenous people."

xref.title: Work in Indigenous Community
xref.body: After graduating, Hurst found a job at Kenna Poaca, a Dakota community in southwest Manitoba, which had sought help for two years. He became deeply involved in the community's indigenous culture for several years, also serving as an instructor for nursing fundamentals. "Trevor became deeply involved in the community's indigenous culture, spending several years there."
